Beaverton is a Washington County city on the eastern edge of the Tualatin Valley, with Portland to the east, Hillsboro to the west and Tigard to the south. The 2020 census counted 97,494 residents, up 8.6 percent from 89,803 in 2010. That makes it the second-largest city in Washington County and the seventh-largest in Oregon.

The city has 13 neighborhoods, among them Central Beaverton, Denney Whitford, Raleigh West, Five Oaks, Triple Creek, Highland, South Beaverton, Vose and West Slope. Buyers here usually talk about a house by its neighborhood and its school boundary. Most of the city is in the Beaverton School District, while portions fall in the Hillsboro School District and Portland Public Schools. Nike is the largest employer, and jobs in the nearby Silicon Forest corridor keep the rental market busy.

Beaverton sellers pay a real estate transfer tax that most Oregon cities cannot charge. Washington County collects $1 per $1,000 of selling price on real property transfers. State law, ORS 306.815, bars most local transfer taxes but carves out taxes already in effect on March 31, 1997, and the county's Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance is Washington County Code Chapter 3.04.

The county's exemption form lists many transfers that are not taxed. A claim must be filed within 15 days of tendering the documents for recording.

  • Transfers by gift, devise or inheritance.
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers in foreclosure or bankruptcy.
  • Transfers between spouses under a court order in a divorce.
  • Conveyances to or from a government entity.
  • Transfers with a selling price of $13,999 or less.

Ask your escrow officer who is paying the tax on your sale and where it appears on the settlement statement.

Washington County Assessment and Taxation bills Beaverton property tax. Taxes can be paid in full or in thirds, and the 3 percent discount for paying in full requires a postmark of November 15.

The statement shows Real Market Value, the estimated sale price as of January 1, and Taxable Value, the lower of market value or maximum assessed value. It lists education, general government, bond and local option levies. Delinquent taxes from earlier years appear on it too, and payments go to the oldest year first. An asterisk beside a property means it is in foreclosure.

Appeals to the Board of Property Tax Appeals are due December 31, and Measure 50 caps growth in assessed value at 3 percent a year. The county's sample tax statement page shows how to read each line.

More than half of Beaverton's occupied homes are rented: 52.5 percent are renter-occupied and 47.5 percent are owner-occupied. Many sellers here are landlords.

ORS 90.427 sets the rules. After a tenant's first year, a landlord who wants to end the tenancy for a sale generally needs an accepted offer from a buyer who will live in the home, and written notice at least 90 days ahead. The landlord also pays one month's rent when delivering the notice, with an exception for owners of four or fewer covered units.

A landlord who breaks these rules can owe the tenant three months' rent plus damages. That risk is why many owners prefer a buyer who takes the house with the lease in place.

Beaverton has wet winters and dry summers, with about 39 inches of rain a year, most of it between October and April. December is the wettest month at 6.53 inches. Snow is minor at about 1.9 inches a year, and heat is the bigger swing: July and August highs run near 80 degrees, and the record high is 115 degrees, set in June.

  • Gutters, downspouts and roof condition matter after a long wet season.
  • Attic insulation and cooling matter more as summer extremes show up.
  • Sloped lots in the hillier parts of the city can mean drainage and retaining wall questions. Elevation runs from about 132 feet to about 698 feet.

A leaking roof or a wet crawl space can stall a financed sale, because the lender's appraiser may flag it. Cash purchases avoid that step.

TriMet's MAX light rail has seven stations in the city: Elmonica/SW 170th Avenue, Merlo Road/SW 158th Avenue, Beaverton Creek, Millikan Way, Beaverton Central, Beaverton Transit Center and Sunset Transit Center. The Blue Line serves all seven and the Red Line serves the last two.

Beaverton Transit Center is TriMet's busiest and is the northern end of WES commuter rail. US 26, the Sunset Highway, links the city to Portland, Hillsboro and the coast, and Oregon 217 runs south through Tigard to I-5.

A house within walking distance of a MAX station is a different product from one that needs a car for every errand. Tell any buyer which one you have.

Roof, drainage and cosmetic repairs are optional in an as-is sale. Oregon's seller disclosure statute, ORS 105.462 to 105.490, can still apply, so ask your title company what you must tell a buyer. A cash buyer will not need a lender's appraisal, so a worn house can close without the repair requests that often come with financing.

Before you list, gather your latest tax statement, find out whether the house is in a rental situation, and ask the escrow officer to show how the transfer tax and the year's property tax will be split on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax when I sell a house in Beaverton?
faqs.a: Yes. Washington County charges $1 per $1,000 of selling price, under Washington County Code Chapter 3.04. Gifts, inheritance and certain foreclosure transfers are exempt.

faqs.q: When is the Beaverton property tax deadline?
faqs.a: November 15 is the key date. Washington County gives a 3 percent discount for full payment postmarked by then, and bills can also be paid in thirds.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix my Beaverton house before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. Roof, drainage and cosmetic repairs are optional in an as-is sale, though Oregon's seller disclosure statute, ORS 105.462 to 105.490, can still apply, so ask your title company.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Beaverton rental with a tenant in it?
faqs.a: Yes, and many owners do. ORS 90.427 limits ending a tenancy for a sale, so a buyer who takes the house with the lease in place avoids the 90-day notice and rent payment rules.

faqs.q: When do I appeal a Beaverton property value?
faqs.a: By December 31, to the Board of Property Tax Appeals. Call Washington County appraisal at 503-846-8826 with questions first.
